nameStory: The delta arrowhead gets its name from its classic arrowhead-shaped leaves and its connection to river deltas in the southeastern United States. Like other arrowheads, the leaves look just like the stone points ancient hunters would tie to their arrows, creating a perfect visual connection between plant and tool.
description: Delta arrowhead is an aquatic plant that grows in shallow water or muddy shores, producing distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that emerge from the water. It's a member of the water-plantain family and produces small white flowers on tall stalks above the foliage. This southeastern native is extremely rare in New England, with only a couple of documented observations in the region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic arrowhead shape with pointed tips and backward-pointing lobes at the base, emerging directly from underwater roots on long, smooth stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with three rounded petals arranged in whorls along a tall, upright stalk that rises well above the leaves

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, delta arrowhead is found in shallow waters of ponds, slow-moving streams, and marshy areas with muddy bottoms. It prefers areas with fluctuating water levels and is typically associated with warmer climates, making any New England occurrence quite noteworthy.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging from underwater rootstocks as water warms, starting as narrow shoots before developing their characteristic arrow shape.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fully developed arrowhead leaves and white flowers blooming on tall stalks above the foliage from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures cool, with the plant storing energy in underground tubers for winter survival.
seasonality.winter: All above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only dormant underground tubers that will sprout again in spring.

funFact: The underground tubers of arrowheads are sometimes called 'duck potatoes' because waterfowl love to dig them up and eat them - and Native Americans traditionally harvested these starchy tubers as an important food source, often wading into marshes to feel for them with their toes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with broadleaf arrowhead, which is much more common in New England. Delta arrowhead typically has broader, more distinctly triangular leaves compared to the narrower arrow shape of broadleaf arrowhead, though this difference can be subtle and requires careful observation.
contextualKnowledge: Delta arrowhead is far outside its typical range in New England - it's primarily a southeastern species. Any sighting in New England should be carefully documented and reported, as it could represent a range extension due to climate change or an unusual introduction.
compareHints: Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead. The leaf shape is the key distinguishing feature, as the flowers of most arrowhead species look quite similar with their three white petals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
